notes.meaning: The word "revelation" means an unveiling, like pulling back a curtain on hidden things. God the Father gave this message to Jesus, and Jesus sent it by His angel to John. It is meant for all of Christ's servants, not only church leaders. The events would begin soon, and they would surely happen.

differ.view: Most of the book is still in the future and will happen just before Christ returns. "Soon" means the events will come suddenly once they start, or that they are near in God's timing.
An older Protestant reading holds that the book traces the church's history from John's day to the end of the world.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars hold that nearly all of the book was fulfilled soon after John wrote it. On this view it describes the fall of Jerusalem and Rome's persecution of Christians.

notes.meaning: John calls himself a witness. He reports faithfully what he saw. He made nothing up, and he held nothing back. What he gives is God's own word and the testimony that Jesus Himself gave.

This is the first of seven blessings in Revelation. In John's day, one person read the book aloud in church while the others listened. The blessing is for those who hear it and also keep it, living by what it says. We may be blessed even when we do not understand every part, because "the time is near."

John greets seven real churches in what is now western Turkey. Seven is the number of fullness, so these churches also stand for the whole church in every age. The blessing comes first from the Father, the eternal God "who is and was and is to come." It also comes from the "seven Spirits," a way of describing the one Holy Spirit in His full and many-sided work.

differ.view: The seven spirits are seven high angels who stand before God's throne.

notes.meaning: Grace also comes from Jesus. He is the faithful witness, whose word we can fully trust. He is the firstborn from the dead, the first to rise and never die again, and He will raise His people too. He rules over every earthly king. He loves us, and by His blood He has set us free from our sins. (Some old copies say "washed us" instead, but both point to the same gift.)

Jesus has made His people a kingdom and priests who serve His Father. As priests, every believer can come near to God directly and offer Him worship and a life given to Him. So John bursts into praise. Glory and power belong to Jesus forever.

This is the theme of the whole book: Jesus is coming again. He will come with the clouds, just as He went up at His ascension. His coming will be personal and seen by everyone. Those who pierced Him will see Him, and so will all who have wounded Him by their sins. Those who have not turned to Him will mourn. "So shall it be" means this is certain.

differ.view: The verse points mainly to Christ coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, punishing those who rejected Him.

notes.meaning: Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. God is the beginning and the end of all things, and everything in between. He is the Almighty, so He is able to do all that this book promises. Some teachers hear the Father speaking here. Others hear Christ, who uses the same titles in verse 17.

John calls himself a brother, not a boss, even though he was an apostle. He shared with the churches in suffering, in Christ's kingdom, and in patient endurance. He had been sent away to Patmos, a small rocky island, because he preached God's word and told people about Jesus. Early writers say this happened under the emperor Domitian.

"The Lord's day" is Sunday, the first day of the week. Christians kept it in honor of Jesus rising from the dead. Cut off from his church, John was still worshiping. God's Spirit took hold of him in a special way and opened his eyes to see visions. Then a voice, loud and clear like a trumpet, broke in behind him.

differ.view: Being "in the Spirit" was not something rare. John was reading, hearing and keeping God's Word in Sunday worship, as any Christian may.

notes.meaning: The voice told John to write down what he saw and send it to seven churches. Each church would hear the whole book, not just its own letter. There were other churches in that area, so the seven also stand for the whole church. The order of the list follows the road a messenger would travel.

differ.view: The seven churches also picture seven ages of church history, from the apostles to the last days.

notes.meaning: John turned to see who was speaking. First he saw seven golden lampstands, which verse 20 says are the churches. A lampstand has no light of its own. It holds up a light. In the same way, churches receive their light from Christ and the gospel and shine it out to others.

Among the lampstands stood "one like the Son of Man": Jesus, in human form but full of glory. This shows that He is always present with His churches. His long robe and golden sash were marks of high rank. Many see them as the dress of a king and of a high priest, the one who stands between God and people.

His snow-white hair echoes the "Ancient of Days" in Daniel 7. It speaks of His majesty, purity and eternity. His eyes like blazing fire see into every heart. They also show His burning anger against sin.

His feet glowed like bronze heated white-hot in a furnace. This pictures His strength and steadiness as He tramples His enemies. His voice roared like ocean waves or a great waterfall. It shows the power of His word, bringing comfort to His friends and terror to His enemies.

The seven stars in His right hand are the leaders of the churches. They are held, guided and protected by Him. The sharp sword coming from His mouth is His word. It cuts deep, judging sin and also healing (Hebrews 4:12). His face shone like the sun at full strength, too bright for human eyes.

John had once leaned on Jesus' chest, yet now he fell down as if dead before such glory. Jesus gently laid His hand on him and said, "Do not be afraid." "The First and the Last" is God's own title in Isaiah. Jesus is eternal, so He can keep every promise.

Jesus is the Living One. He truly died on the cross, and now He lives forever. Keys are a sign of authority. He holds the keys of Death and of Hades, which means the unseen world of the dead. Because He has beaten death, His people need not fear it.

John is to write three things. "What you have seen" is this vision of Christ. "The things that are" are the present state of the churches in chapters 2 and 3. "What will happen after this" is the future shown in the rest of the book.

Jesus explains the hidden meaning, or "mystery," of the picture. The lampstands are the seven churches. The stars are the "angels" of the churches. The word "angel" means messenger, and here it most likely means the minister who leads each church. Christ holds them in His hand and holds them responsible.

differ.view: The "angel" of each church is its bishop, the chief overseer over the other church leaders.
The "angel" is the pastor of a single congregation, not a bishop over many churches.
The "angels" are real heavenly angels who watch over each church.
